extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and students writing mathematical exposition (papers, books, lectures)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing clear, correct, and readable mathematical exposition (theorems, proofs, definitions, lectures, and papers). Emphasizes clarity, honesty about status of claims, correct use of words/symbols, organization, and practical stylistic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty is the best policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the status of statements and your attitude toward them; avoid glossing over difficulties or concealing whether something is proved, unproved, expected, or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose of good mathematical language is to make the subject easy to understand; clarity, not pedantry. If a proof is cumbersome, say so (e.g. 'unfortunately the only known proof is the following cumbersome computation'). If you cannot derive something, confess or promise a counterexample later. When you call something 'obvious' be sure you thought it through and that it is true; don't use 'obvious' as bluff. Always tell the reader where a statement 'stands' (has been proved, will be proved, is false, etc.). Complete honesty makes for greatest clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Down with the irrelevant and the trivial
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid introducing irrelevant hypotheses, irrelevant notation, or irrelevant emphasis that distracts or misleads the reader; treat and mention trivial cases explicitly when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrelevant assumptions (or unnecessary hypotheses) cause confusion (example: mentioning semisimplicity and a unit when irrelevant). If trivial cases are being excluded or handled separately, state that explicitly so the reader is not cheated. Avoid legalistic but misleading insistence on technical correctness that obscures the main idea. Organize so that irrelevant hypotheses are not wantonly dragged in.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the theorem first; the statement should be short
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the theorem statement before comments, definitions, motivation, and proof; ideally the statement is a single, short sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't ramble before announcing what you will prove — the reader follows the proof better when they know the goal and where hypotheses are used. Avoid putting 'Without loss of generality...' or references to other results inside the statement. If a theorem needs an unwieldy list of hypotheses or conclusions, that usually indicates an underlying concept that should be isolated and named instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do and do not repeat
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repetition purposefully: repeat definitions or statements to emphasize important parallels, but avoid word-for-word or needless repetition that confuses or frightens the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good repetition (re-stating a definition where it is needed, using a 'roll of drums' to emphasize a crucial distinction) helps; bad repetition (restating the same words or phrases unnecessarily, or repeating proofs/claims so the reader wonders if they're identical) distracts. Rewriting earlier chapters/sections to create useful parallels is often necessary. Avoid shorthand references like 'see proof of Theorem 1' when the connection is not explicit — extract and present common lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: The editorial 'we' is not all bad
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'we' to mean the author and reader (or coauthors) sensibly; avoid gratuitous uses of 'I' or impersonal 'one' and do not use 'we' to claim joint authorship falsely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the neutral approach: simple declarative sentences are best ('This implies p'). 'We' is useful when it really denotes the author plus the reader (e.g., 'Using Lemma 2 we can generalize...'). Avoid 'Our work was done in 1969' for a single author or 'We thank our wife...' which is inappropriate. The imperative can be an effective device ('Given p, put q equal to r'), but don't use it when it means nothing or leaves 'given' dangling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use words correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words with precise logical meaning to avoid changing mathematical content (e.g., avoid ambiguous 'any', use 'each' or 'every' when universal quantification is meant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to small but important words: 'any' can be ambiguous (existential vs universal), 'where' often indicates lazy afterthought, 'equivalent' is often misused. Avoid recoding plain prose into formal logic unnecessarily; prefer clarity for human readers. Recast sentences that obscure logical structure and ensure phrases reflect intended quantifiers and dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms correctly and consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain and respect standard distinctions among technical terms (e.g., 'function' vs 'value', 'sequence' vs 'countable set', 'contain' vs 'include'), and be consistent in terminology and notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misuse of technical words slows the reader and can cause misunderstanding. Create new terms only when necessary, consult references (e.g., Roget) for phrasing, and use existing terms correctly and consistently. Consistency across notation, references, and typography is a major virtue; its absence is a cardinal sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer prose to heavy notation; use symbols only when they materially aid clarity, and avoid superfluous letters or displays that make reading harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best notation is no notation. Avoid irrelevant symbols (example: unnecessary 'p' or '/' in displays) and avoid leaving free variables dangling. Replace long chains of algebraic equalities with a short explanatory paragraph describing the idea of the manipulation. Avoid backward proofs that are machine-verifiable but hard to follow; write forward, explain the reasoning, and include small illustrative cases when helpful (e.g., prove a typical 3x3 case instead of a messy general matrix computation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbols correctly (consistently and punctuate symbolic sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use each symbol consistently (know whether a symbol reads as 'is in' or 'in') and punctuate symbolic or displayed mathematical sentences as you would verbal ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on and keep a consistent reading for symbols (e.g., read '∈' as 'is in'). Don't over-label displays or attach labels unnecessarily — labels attract attention and can create unfounded expectations. Punctuate symbolic sentences (commas, periods) to avoid forcing readers to backtrack. Use 'then' with 'if' in mathematical contexts to aid readability. Be stingy but reasonable with labeled displays; parsimony avoids distraction but extremal parsimony can frustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermix prose and displays appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Break up symbolic material with enough prose to help the reader's eye and brain; avoid pages that look like computational hash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersperse displays so the printed page isn't all symbols; prose guides intuition and memory. Avoid excessive suffixes, indices, or chained notation that drowns the exposition. The golden mean is to use enough displays to aid comprehension but keep them embedded in explanatory prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: All communication is exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat papers, lectures, and other forms of communication as instances of exposition with common goals: content, aim, organization, grammar, diction, and notation must be adapted to the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While particulars differ (a lecture requires more omission and oral pacing; a reader can pause and resume), the basic problems are the same. Plan lectures differently from papers: a hearer cannot 'pick up the thread' later as easily as a reader. Use omission and emphasis appropriately according to medium; the same stylistic rules (clarity, organization, attention to detail) apply to all formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend your style
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to defend your technical and stylistic choices against copyreaders or editors who may introduce incorrect mechanical 'corrections'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial assistants can help but they may also introduce serious errors (e.g., removing a necessary hyphen and producing 'nonmeasure preserving' instead of 'non-measure-preserving'). Know the logical punctuation/formatting decisions (quotation marks and adjacent punctuation) and be willing to argue or correct editorial changes that change meaning. Carry examples and reasoning to preserve mathematically significant stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop (finish your writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when to stop improving and finish the manuscript; avoid endless tinkering in pursuit of illusory perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author's final task is to stop writing and declare the work finished; continual revisions for marginal improvements can prevent completion. Accept that some imperfections remain and submit/finish when the work has been sufficiently improved.
